body.text: Headlines for the big show business award ceremonies follow a few basic conventions: the show that sweeps the board; the controversial speech; the breakout newcomer or returning veteran; the record-breaking win.

This year’s Emmys saw two firsts. Jean Smart set a record with five successive wins for a lead role in every season of a single series. Hacks, in which she plays an ageing comedian making a comeback, is a genuine tour de force for an actor whose career went from regional rep to Broadway, followed by a diverse range of successes in television comedy.

One of the problems for TV awards is that the cast of last year’s runaway success are left grinning awkwardly in their seats while this year’s awards pass them by, so Smart’s persistent return to the platform is a welcome break in the pattern. Keri Russell, after starring in three seasons of The Diplomat to widespread acclaim, missed out on an award but responded with convincing enthusiasm to husband Matthew Rhys’s double win as best actor in a limited or anthology series for The Beast in Me and in comedy for Widow’s Bay.

Widow’s Bay was the story of the night with a total of fourteen wins including supporting actor and actress, writing, directing, cinematography, music and editing. Sometimes success has a momentum of its own that adds a delusory gloss: Widow’s Bay is entertaining enough and builds to a strong final episode, but is not as original as the hype suggests.

Horror and comedy are long-established companions, and the haunted island story was, for my money, done with more genuine dramatic power in Midnight Mass (2021), which got no nods from the Emmys. Hamish Linklater, who won a Critics Choice Award for a complex and compelling performance in the lead role in that series, was nominated for a guest role as the demonic pastor in Widow’s Bay. He didn’t win.

The seventy-eight Primetime Emmys took place in a year that has seen the ninety-eighth Oscars, the eighty-third Golden Globes, the seventy-ninth BAFTAs and, here in Australia, the sixty-sixth Logies. Is it longevity alone that keeps these bizarre extravaganzas from fading away? Ratings for the Emmys have held up well in comparison with the Oscars and Globes. Streaming services offering an increasing range of film and television drama have drawn audiences away from the cinema.

The ceremonies, though, are trapped in a genre of their own. The frock parade on the red carpet is here to stay, along with the teary speeches that make you wonder how good actors can give such excruciatingly bad performances when they try to be themselves. As lists of awards get longer, the litany of thankyous tries the patience of any viewer, while the captive celebrity audience feel nothing but the pain of their corsets and pinching shoes.

While the show itself may be the ostensible drawcard — the Emmys are still proclaimed as “television’s night of nights” — it might actually be a burden sustained in the service of other purposes. Images from the red carpet generate high-volume traffic through the internet, sustaining an essential promotion platform for the fashion industry. Major awards create star power, which is literally bankable in the wider show business economy.

History, though, provides a story with a different kind of emphasis. The Emmys are awarded by the Academy of Television Arts and Sciences whose founder, Syd Cassyd, worked as a film editor during the second world war under Frank Capra, then a colonel in the Army Signal Corps.

Cassyd became a passionate advocate for the new medium of television as a means of providing public information and entertainment. Star power was the last thing on his mind when he founded the Academy with the aim of bringing together representatives of all the technical and professional skills involved in visual broadcasting.

The inaugural Emmy Awards in 1949 recognised popularity and personality, but the technical side of things was to the fore. The statue, designed by a television engineer, took its name from the “Immy” or image-orthicon camera tube and portrayed a nymph holding aloft a sphere representing an atom.

Since then, the range of awards has proliferated along with the development of programs making ever more sophisticated demands in all areas of production. There are now over one hundred Emmys across twenty-eight fields, with three ceremonies culminating in the major acting and drama presentations that bring the celebrities out in force.

But aside from the performance categories that get the headlines, separate divisions for drama, comedy series, limited anthology or movie, animation, reality competition and variety series serve to multiply awards in other areas. Music score, script writing, visual and sound editing, sound design, voice over, camera work, costume, casting, choreography, lighting, make up, hairstyling, production design, set dressing: all have their own subdivisions.

There is real importance in the recognition that these are specialized areas involving innovation, aesthetic judgement and the most exacting craft. A breakout success tends to happen when they all converge at a very high level, and the focus on craft carries through to the higher profile awards.

Rhea Seehorn accepted the award for best actress in a drama series in Pluribus with a speech highlighting the whole-of-production teamwork behind an on-screen performance in which she is the central focus in every scene. Pluribus, the brainchild of Breaking Bad creator Vince Gilligan, takes the risk of stranding its central character in solitude after a strange viral invasion leaves most of humanity as mental automatons.

This places an immense burden not just on the star but also on the crew responsible for creating an environment with rhythmic sound and image montage that moves the story in unorthodox ways. The show was nominated for eighteen awards, most of them in “below the line” production categories, and though most of these didn’t translate into wins, they drew attention to its scenic innovation, including the creation of a translucent ice hotel.

Series favoured by the Emmys are often genre-defying, taking commercial risks with dramatic explorations of the tougher and stranger aspects of human experience. Another standout this year was The Pitt, a medical drama set in an emergency ward that could at times be mistaken for reality TV. In competition with Pluribus, The Pitt won the overall category award for outstanding drama series, with production wins in casting and make-up.

As an awards show junky from my teenage years, I’m usually left at the end of the Oscars night with that feeling you get after eating the whole packet of Tim Tams. The Emmys manage to sustain a genuinely different register, in which “Academy” means more than celebrity. •
